      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Anxiety</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Generalized <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Disorder</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Anxiety</span> is a feeling of fear, dread, and uneasiness. It might cause you to sweat, feel restless and <span class="qt1">tense</span>, and have a rapid heartbeat.   It can be a normal reaction to <span class="qt1">stress</span>. For example, you might feel <span class="qt1">anxious</span> when faced with a difficult problem at work, before taking a test, or before making an important decision. It can help you to cope. The <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> may give you a boost of energy or help you focus. But for people with <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>, the fear is not temporary and can be overwhelming.</p>What are <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>?<p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">Anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span> are conditions in which you have <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> that does not go away and can get worse over time. The symptoms can interfere with daily activities such as job performance, schoolwork, and relationships.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>?<p>There are several types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>, including: </p><ul><li>Generalized <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorder</span></span> (GAD). People with GAD worry about ordinary issues such as health, money, work, and family. But their worries are excessive, and they have them almost every day for at least 6 months.</li><li>Panic <span class="qt2">disorder</span>. People with panic <span class="qt2">disorder</span> have panic attacks. These are sudden, repeated periods of intense fear when there is no danger. The attacks come on quickly and can last several minutes or more.</li><li>Phobias. People with phobias have an intense fear of something that poses little or no actual danger. Their fear may be about spiders, flying, going to crowded places, or being in social situations (known as social <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>).</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>?<p>The cause of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> is unknown. Factors such as genetics, brain biology and chemistry, <span class="qt1">stress</span>, and your environment may play a role.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>?<p>The risk factors for the different types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span> can vary. For example, GAD and phobias are more common in women, but social <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> affects men and women equally. There are some <span class="qt0">general</span> risk factors for all types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>, including:</p><ul><li>Certain personality traits, such as being shy or withdrawn when you are in new situations or meeting new people</li><li>Traumatic events in early childhood or adulthood</li><li>Family history of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> or other mental <span class="qt2">disorders</span></li><li>Some physical health conditions, such as thyroid problems or arrhythmia</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>?<p>The different types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span> can have different symptoms. But they all have a combination of:</p><ul><li><span class="qt1">Anxious</span> thoughts or beliefs that are hard to control. They make you feel restless and <span class="qt1">tense</span> and interfere with your daily life. They do not go away and can get worse over time.</li><li>Physical symptoms, such as a pounding or rapid heartbeat, unexplained aches and pains, dizziness, and shortness of breath</li><li>Changes in behavior, such as avoiding everyday activities you used to do</li></ul><p>Using caffeine, other substances, and certain medicines can make your symptoms worse.</p>How are <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. You may also have a physical exam and lab tests to make sure that a different health problem is not the cause of your symptoms.</p><p>If you don't have another health problem, you will get a psychological evaluation. Your provider may do it, or you may be referred to a mental health professional to get one.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>?<p>The main treatments for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span> are psychotherapy (talk therapy), medicines, or both:</p><ul><li>Psychotherapy can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. To be effective, it should focus on your specific <span class="qt1">anxieties</span> and needs. There are many types; some of the types used for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span> include:
  <ul><li>Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which teaches you different ways of thinking and behaving. It can help you change how you react to the things that cause you to feel fear and <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>. It may include exposure therapy. This therapy focuses on having you confront your fears so that you will be able to do the things that you had been avoiding.</li><li>Acceptance and commitment therapy may help with some <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>. It uses strategies such as mindfulness and goal setting to reduce discomfort and <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>.</li></ul> 
</li><li>Medicines to treat <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span> include anti-<span class="qt1">anxiety</span> medicines and certain antidepressants. Some types of medicines may work better for specific types of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">anxiety</span></span><span class="qt3"> </span><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">disorders</span></span>. You should work closely with your provider to identify which medicine is best for you. You may need to try more than one medicine before you can find the right one.</li></ul><p>Support groups and <span class="qt1">stress</span> management techniques may also be helpful.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/sleepdisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Sleep <span class="qt2">Disorders</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Narcolepsy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Night Terrors</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sleeping Pills</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is sleep?<p>While you are sleeping  your brain and body functions are still active. Sleep is a natural process that helps your body restore energy, supports learning and memory, and keeps you healthy.</p><p>It's not just the number of hours of sleep you get that matters. The quality of your sleep is also important. During the night, your brain cycles through different stages of non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. If your sleep is often interrupted, you may not get enough time in certain stages of sleep. Poor-quality sleep does more than make you feel tired. It can affect your physical and mental health, thinking, and daily functioning.</p>What are sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span>?<p>Sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span> are conditions that disturb your normal sleep patterns. There are many types of sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span>. Some <span class="qt0">general</span> types include:</p><ul><li>Insomnia, which is trouble falling asleep or staying asleep.</li><li>Sleep-related breathing <span class="qt2">disorders</span> such as sleep apnea, a condition in which you stop breathing for 10 seconds or more during sleep.</li><li>Sleep-related movement <span class="qt2">disorders</span> such as restless leg syndrome (RLS), which involves tingling or prickling sensations in your legs, and a strong urge to move them.</li><li>Hypersomnia, which is extreme daytime sleepiness. This includes narcolepsy.</li><li>Circadian rhythm sleep-wake <span class="qt2">disorders</span>, which are problems falling asleep or waking up at the right times. This may be due to shift work or jet lag.</li><li>Parasomnia, which is unusual behaviors during sleep or while falling asleep or waking up. This may include sleepwalking, talking, or eating during sleep.</li></ul><p>Some people who feel tired during the day have a true sleep <span class="qt2">disorder</span>, while others simply don't get enough sleep. The amount of sleep you need depends on your age, lifestyle, health, and sleep patterns. Most adults need about 7-9 hours each night.</p>What causes sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span>?<p>There are different causes for different sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span>. They may include:</p><ul><li>Other health conditions, such as heart disease, lung disease, nerve <span class="qt2">disorders</span>, or pain</li><li>Mental illnesses, including depression and <span class="qt1">anxiety</span></li><li>Medicines</li><li>Genetics</li></ul><p>Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p><p>Other factors that may contribute to sleep problems include:</p><ul><li>Using caffeine or alcohol</li><li>Having an irregular schedule, such as working the night shift</li><li>Aging, since older adults may sleep less, spend less time in deep sleep, and wake easily</li></ul>What are the symptoms of sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span>?<p>The symptoms of sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span> depend on the specific <span class="qt2">disorder</span>. Some signs that you may have a sleep <span class="qt2">disorder</span> include that:</p><ul><li>You regularly take more than 30 minutes to fall asleep.</li><li>You regularly wake up several times and then have trouble falling back to sleep, or you wake up too early in the morning.</li><li>You often feel sleepy during the day, take frequent naps, or fall asleep at the wrong times during the day.</li><li>Your bed partner says that when you sleep, you snore loudly, snort, gasp, make choking sounds, or stop breathing for short periods.</li><li>You have creeping or tingling sensations in your legs or arms that are relieved by moving or massaging them, especially in the evening and when trying to fall asleep.</li><li>Your bed partner notices that your legs or arms jerk often during sleep.</li><li>You have vivid, dreamlike experiences while falling asleep or dozing.</li><li>You have episodes of sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions.</li><li>You feel as though you cannot move or speak for a brief time when you first wake up.</li></ul>How are sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span> diagnosed?<p>To diagnose a sleep <span class="qt2">disorder</span>, your health care provider will review your medical and sleep history and do a physical exam. You may also have a sleep study (polysomnogram). Most sleep studies  monitor and record data about your body during a full night of sleep. The data includes:</p><ul><li>Brain wave activity</li><li>Eye movements</li><li>Breathing rate</li><li>Blood pressure</li><li>Heart rate and electrical activity in the heart and other muscles</li></ul><p>Other types of sleep studies may check how quickly you fall asleep during daytime naps or how well you can stay awake during the day.</p>What are the treatments for sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span>?<p>Treatments for sleep <span class="qt2">disorders</span> depend on which <span class="qt2">disorder</span> you have. They may include:</p><ul><li>Practicing good sleep habits and other lifestyle changes, such as eating a healthy diet and getting regular exercise</li><li>Reducing <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> about sleep with cognitive behavioral therapy or relaxation techniques</li><li>Using a CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine for sleep apnea</li><li>Using bright light therapy (in the morning)</li><li>Taking sleep aid medicines, or natural products such as melatonin</li></ul><p>Always check with your provider before taking any medicine or supplement. Most sleep aid medicines are generally for short-term use.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/depression.html">
      <content name="title">Depression</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dysthymic <span class="qt2">Disorder</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Clinical depression</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Major depressive <span class="qt2">disorder</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Unipolar depression</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is depression?<p>Depression is more than a feeling of being sad or irritable for a few days. It's a serious mood <span class="qt2">disorder</span>. As one of the most common mental <span class="qt2">disorders</span> in the United States, depression can affect how you think, feel, and your everyday life. You may not know why you feel this way, but even basic daily activities such as sleeping, eating, or working may become difficult. Depression often needs long-term treatment but getting help at the earliest sign of a problem can help manage your symptoms.</p>What are the different types of depression?<p>The most common types of depression are major depression and persistent depressive <span class="qt2">disorder</span>.</p><ul><li>Major depression symptoms include a depressed mood or a loss of interest. Symptoms affect your daily activities and last for at least two weeks.</li><li>Persistent depressive <span class="qt2">disorder</span> (also called dysthymia or dysthymic <span class="qt2">disorder</span>) has less severe depressive symptoms, but they last longer, usually for at least two years.</li></ul><p>Other types of depression can include:</p><ul><li>Seasonal affective <span class="qt2">disorder</span> comes and goes with the seasons. It usually starts in late fall and early winter and goes away during the spring and summer.</li><li>Bipolar <span class="qt2">disorder</span> is sometimes called manic depression. This mood <span class="qt2">disorder</span> can cause intense mood swings.</li><li>Depression with symptoms of psychosis is a severe form of depression that also has delusions (false beliefs) or hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or feeling something that isn't there).</li></ul>What causes depression?<p>There are a variety of things that may cause depression, including genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors. Depression can happen at any age and can affect anyone, but it's more common in women. This is often due to the physical and hormonal changes that women have during menstruation, pregnancy, the postpartum period, and menopause. Other mental <span class="qt2">disorders</span> or chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, cancer, or heart disease may occur with depression. This may make the chronic condition or depression worse.</p><p>In some cases, there is no clear cause for depression.</p>Who is at risk of depression?<p>You may be at a higher risk of depression if you have a close relative who has it or another mental health <span class="qt2">disorder</span>. Going through trauma or stressful life events may raise your risk even more.</p>What are the symptoms of depression?<p>Depression doesn't look the same on everyone. The type and number of symptoms of depression can vary and don't always appear like sadness. Depression may affect you differently based on your:</p><ul><li>Age. The symptoms of depression may be different in a child, who may appear more irritable than sad. Teens may act out or have excessive sleepiness. The symptoms for an older adult may not be as obvious as other age groups.</li><li>Sex. Men often show symptoms and coping behaviors differently than women. Rather than sad, men may appear angry or irritable.</li><li>Medical conditions. Some medicines and medical conditions may cause symptoms that look like depression. Chronic conditions may make depression worse.</li></ul><p>Symptoms of depression are ongoing and affect your day-to-day life. They can include:</p><ul><li>Feeling sad or "empty"</li><li>Losing interest in favorite activities</li><li>Overeating, or not wanting to eat at all</li><li>Sleeping too much, or not enough</li><li>Feeling very tired</li><li>Feeling hopeless, irritable, <span class="qt1">anxious</span>, or guilty</li><li>Having aches and pains, headaches, cramps, or digestive problems</li><li>Having thoughts of death or suicide</li><li>Changing moods or behaviors</li><li>Increasing use of alcohol or drugs</li><li>Isolating from family and friends</li></ul>How is depression diagnosed?<p>If you think you have depression, talk to your health care provider or a mental health provider. To be diagnosed with depression, your provider may use many tools:</p><ul><li>A medical history will include asking about your symptoms and family history. To be diagnosed with depression, your symptoms must occur most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. One of the symptoms must be a depressed mood or a loss of interest in most activities.</li><li>Medical tests may be done to rule out other medical conditions. Certain medicines and medical conditions (such as viruses or thyroid <span class="qt2">disorders</span>) may cause symptoms like depression.</li><li>A physical exam to make sure another issue isn't causing your symptoms.</li><li>A mental health evaluation by your provider or a mental health provider.</li></ul>What are the treatments for depression?<p>Depression may need long-term treatment. Most treatments include medicines and/or psychotherapy (talk therapy):</p><ul><li>Medicines such as antidepressants may help control your symptoms. You may need to try several medicines to find which works best for you. Medicine may take time to work and can have side effects. Don't stop taking your medicine without first talking with your provider. Contact your provider if you have any concerns about side effects from the medicine.</li><li>Psychotherapy (talk therapy) under the care of a mental health provider can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. This may be done one-on-one or in a group setting. It can give you and your family support, education, skills, and coping strategies.</li><li>Light therapy has been shown to be effective for seasonal affective <span class="qt2">disorder</span> (SAD).</li><li>Other treatments options may be considered if treatment isn't working or if depression is severe. These may include:
	<ul><li>Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses a mild electric current when you are under <span class="qt0">general</span> anesthesia. ECT is most often used for severe depression that is not getting better with other treatments.</li><li>Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a brain stimulation procedure that uses magnetic waves to relieve depression. It's not as powerful as ECT, but with rTMS, you don't need anesthesia. It also has a low risk of negative effects on your memory and thinking.</li></ul>
</li></ul>Can depression be prevented?<p>Most cases of depression can't be prevented, but healthy lifestyle changes can have long-term benefits for your mental health. These can include:</p><ul><li>Getting regular exercise</li><li>Having a consistent sleep schedule</li><li>Controlling <span class="qt1">stress</span></li></ul><p>If you, or someone you love is depressed, see your provider or a mental health provider. It's important to get treatment at the earliest sign of a problem.</p><p>If you or someone you know has thoughts of hurting themselves or attempting suicide, get help right away. If it is an emergency, dial 911.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/polycysticovarysyndrome.html">
      <content name="title">Polycystic Ovary Syndrome</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">PCOS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Stein-Leventhal Syndrome</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)? <p>Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), also known as polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome (PMOS), is the name of a hormonal <span class="qt2">disorder</span>. PCOS affects the ovaries, as well as many other parts of the body.</p><p>If you have PCOS, you usually have at least two of these problems:</p><ul><li>Not ovulating. Normally, your ovaries make the egg that is released each month as part of a healthy menstrual cycle. This is called ovulation. But with PCOS, the egg may not develop as it should, or it may not be released during ovulation. Your periods may be irregular, or you may not have them at all.</li><li>High levels of androgens. Androgens are hormones that are important for normal male sexual development. Women normally make smaller amounts of androgens. Having higher levels of androgens can cause you to have extra body or facial hair (called hirsutism).</li><li>Growths in one or both ovaries. These growths are often clumps of ovarian follicles that have stopped developing. They may appear as cysts, which are small fluid-filled sacs</li></ul><p>Although it's less common, you may not have growths in your ovaries. You may only have symptoms of PCOS, not ovulate, and have high levels of androgens.</p>What causes polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>The exact cause of PCOS is unknown. Research has shown that different factors may play a role, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics. PCOS tends to run in families.</li><li>Imbalances in androgen levels.</li><li>Insulin resistance. This is a condition in which your body can't use insulin properly. Insulin is a hormone that helps move blood glucose (also called blood sugar) into your cells to give them energy. Insulin resistance can lead to high blood glucose levels.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS often develops as young as age 11 or 12, around the time of your first period. But you can develop it later.</p><p>The symptoms can vary from person to person. Some women have few or even no symptoms. They may not realize they have PCOS until they have trouble getting pregnant. Other women may have more severe symptoms.</p><p>The symptoms of PCOS may include:</p><ul><li>Irregular or missed menstrual periods.</li><li>Too much hair on the face, chest, stomach, or thighs.</li><li>Obesity, weight gain, or trouble losing weight.</li><li>Severe acne which may be hard to treat.</li><li>Oily skin.</li><li>Patches of thickened dark skin (called acanthosis nigricans).</li><li>Infertility. PCOS is one of the most common causes of infertility. But many women with PCOS can still get pregnant.</li></ul>What other health problems are linked to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS is linked to many other health problems, including:</p><ul><li>Insulin resistance, which can lead to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.</li><li>Heart disease. Having PCOS increases your risk, and this risk goes up as you age.</li><li>High blood pressure.</li><li>High LDL ("bad") cholesterol and low HDL ("good") cholesterol. This increases your risk of heart disease.</li><li>Endometrial hyperplasia, a condition in which the lining of your uterus, or womb, becomes too thick. This can increase your risk for endometrial cancer, also called uterine cancer.</li><li>Sleep apnea, a <span class="qt2">disorder</span> that causes you to repeatedly stop breathing during sleep.</li><li>Depression and <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>.</li></ul><p>Although there are links between PCOS and these conditions, researchers do not know whether:</p><ul><li>PCOS causes some of these problems</li><li>Some of these problems cause PCOS, OR</li><li>There are other conditions that cause both PCOS and these other health problems</li></ul><p>Not everyone who has PCOS will have all these problems. However, you and your health care provider may want to monitor your health for signs of them, so they can be treated early.</p>How is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for PCOS. To find out if you have PCOS, your provider: </p><ul><li>Will do a physical exam, which will include looking for the physical signs of PCOS.</li><li>Will ask about your medical history and family health history.</li><li>May do a pelvic exam to check for signs of extra male hormones and to see if your ovaries are enlarged or swollen.</li><li>May order a pelvic ultrasound to look for growths on your ovaries and check the thickness of your endometrium (the lining of your uterus, or womb).</li><li>May order blood tests, including tests to check your hormone levels.</li></ul>What are the treatments for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>Treatments for PCOS can help you manage your symptoms. The treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes, which can help reduce many symptoms. They can also lower your risk for or help manage related health problems. These changes include:
  <ul><li>Maintaining a healthy weight</li><li>Getting regular physical activity</li><li>Eating healthy foods</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicines:<ul><li>Hormonal birth control, such as pills, shots, and IUDs, can make your period more regular. They may also help remove acne and extra facial and body hair. But it's only an option if you're not currently trying to get pregnant.</li><li>Anti-androgen medicines, which block the effect of androgens. This can help reduce hair loss on your head, the growth of facial and body hair, and acne. Providers do use them to help with these symptoms, but anti-androgen medicines are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat PCOS. These medicines can cause problems during pregnancy. Your provider may have you take them with birth control (to prevent pregnancy).</li><li>Insulin-sensitizing medicines, which are medicines that are used to treat type 2 diabetes. They improve insulin resistance and keep your blood glucose levels steady. They may also lower your androgen levels. They are not approved by the FDA to treat PCOS. But they may help with your symptoms.</li><li>Medicines for acne. These medicines come in pills, creams, or gels.</li></ul></li><li>Treatments for hair removal, such as facial hair removal creams, laser hair removal, and electrolysis.</li><li>Fertility treatments if you are having trouble getting pregnant. They include medicines and procedures such as in vitro fertilization (IVF).</li></ul></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Sleep Hygiene</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is sleep?<p>While you are sleeping your brain and body functions are still active. Sleep is a natural process that helps your body restore energy, supports learning and memory, and keeps you healthy.</p><p>During sleep, your brain cycles through different stages of non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Non-REM sleep has three stages that range from light to deep sleep, while REM sleep is when most dreaming occurs. During each stage, your brain waves, breathing, heart rate, and body temperature change throughout the night.  Certain phases of sleep help you:</p><ul><li>Feel rested and energetic the next day.</li><li>Learn new information, get insight, and form memories.</li><li>Give your heart and blood vessels a rest.</li><li>Release growth hormone, which helps children grow and assists in muscle repair and tissue healing for everyone.</li><li>Release sex hormones, which contribute to puberty and fertility.</li><li>Maintain a healthy balance of hormones that control hunger and fullness.</li><li>Strengthen your immune system by producing cytokines (hormones that help the body fight infection).</li></ul><p>You need all the stages to get a healthy sleep.</p>How much sleep do I need?<p>The amount of sleep you need depends on your age, lifestyle, health, and sleep patterns. The <span class="qt0">general</span> recommendations for sleep are:</p><ul><li>Babies (4-12 months): 12-16 hours a day (including naps)</li><li>Children (1-2 years): 11-14 hours a day (including naps)</li><li>Children (3-5 years): 10-13 hours a day (including naps)</li><li>Children (6-12 years): 9-12 hours a day</li><li>Teens (13-18 years): 8-10 hours a day</li><li>Adults (18 years and older): 7-9 hours a day</li></ul><p>During puberty, teenagers' biological clocks shift. They tend to fall asleep later and wake up later, which can conflict with the early school start times. This is one reason many teenagers don't get enough sleep.</p><p>Some people think adults need less sleep as they age, but there is no evidence to support this. However, older adults often get less sleep or spend less time in the deep, restful stages of sleep. They also wake up more easily.</p><p>It's not just the number of hours of sleep you get that matters. The quality of the sleep you get is also important. People whose sleep is frequently interrupted might not get enough of certain stages of sleep. 
If you are wondering whether you are getting enough sleep, including quality sleep, ask yourself:</p><ul><li>Do I have trouble getting up in the morning?</li><li>Do I have trouble focusing during the day?</li><li>Do I doze off during the day?</li></ul><p>If you answered yes to any of these questions, you may need to improve your sleep habits.</p>What are the health effects of not getting enough sleep?<p>Sleep is important for overall health. When you don't get enough sleep (sleep deprivation), it does more than just make you feel tired. It can impair your ability to think clearly, react quickly, and form memories. This increases your risk of making mistakes, taking risks, or getting into accidents.</p><p>Sleep deprivation can also affect your mood, leading to:</p><ul><li>Irritability</li><li>Problems with relationships, especially for children and teenagers</li><li>Depression</li><li><span class="qt1">Anxiety</span></li></ul><p>It can also affect your physical health. Not getting enough sleep, or getting poor-quality sleep, increases your risk of:</p><ul><li>High blood pressure</li><li>Heart disease</li><li>Stroke</li><li>Kidney disease</li><li>Obesity</li><li>Type 2 diabetes</li></ul><p>Not getting enough sleep can also lower your levels of hormones that help children grow and help the body build muscle, repair tissue, and fight infections.</p><p>Sleep deprivation also magnifies the effect of alcohol. A tired person who drinks too much alcohol will be more impaired than a well-rested person who drinks the same amount.</p>How can I get better sleep?<p>You can take steps to improve your sleep habits. First, make sure that you allow yourself enough time for sleep. Getting enough sleep each night may help you feel happier and more productive during the day.</p><p>To improve your sleep habits, it also may help to:</p><ul><li>Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.</li><li>Avoid caffeine, especially in the afternoon and evening.</li><li>Avoid nicotine.</li><li>Exercise regularly, but not too close to bedtime.</li><li>Avoid alcoholic drinks before bed.</li><li>Avoid large meals and drinks late at night.</li><li>Don't take a nap after 3 p.m.</li><li>Relax before bed by taking a bath, reading or listening to calm music.</li><li>Keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet.</li><li>Get rid of distractions such as TVs, computers, and phones.</li><li>Get enough sunlight exposure during the day.</li><li>If you can't fall asleep for 20 minutes, get up and do something relaxing.</li><li>See a health care provider if you have continued trouble sleeping. You may have a sleep <span class="qt2">disorder</span>, such as insomnia or sleep apnea. In some cases, your provider may suggest trying a sleep study or other treatments.</li></ul><p>If you are a shift worker, getting good sleep can be more challenging. You may also want to:</p><ul><li>Take naps and extend your total sleep time</li><li>Keep the lights bright at work</li><li>Limit shift changes to help your body adjust</li><li>Limit caffeine to the first part of your shift</li><li>Remove sound and light distractions in your bedroom during daytime sleep (for example, use light-blocking curtains or earplugs)</li></ul></content>
